title: Five years: the banis
hookLine: Japji, Jaap, Anand, Rehras, Sohila, Sukhmani, the Var at dawn
tomorrow: how does a village on a riverbank end up in Simran's California?

cards: Twenty minutes on the school bus, earbuds in, nothing playing. That's the quietest part of Simran's day now, with the send-off coming and finals stacked behind it. So she makes a playlist with no music in it.
One line from each of the banis she's met, the Guru's words she's prayed over the years, said under her breath between stops.

teach.b: Here's her list, in the original Punjabi, with the sense. Japji: aad sach, jugaad sach, true in the beginning, true through the ages.

teach.h: NO MARK, NO COLOR, NO CASTE.
teach.b: Jaap: chakkar chihan ar baran jaat ar paat nahin jih, the One has no mark, no color, no caste.

teach.h: BLISS HAS COME, O MY MOTHER.
teach.b: Anand: anand bhaiaa meri maae, bliss has come, O my mother. Rehras: so dar keha, what is that door, where everything sings.

teach.h: THE HOUSE WHERE PRAISE IS SUNG.
teach.b: Sohila: jai ghar keerat aakheeai, in the house where praise is sung. Sukhmani: sukhmani sukh amrit prabh naam, the Name is peace and nectar. And the Var at dawn, Asa di Var: balihaari gur aapne, I give myself to my Guru.
That Jaap line is worth a second look: before it says what the One is, it says what the One isn't, and it starts by taking away the labels people use to rank each other.
And on one bus ride, Simran hears several Gurus, from the first to the tenth. Notice the shape too.
Banis aren't one long prayer. They frame a day: dawn, evening, the edge of sleep. Simran gets off the bus with seven lines and a day already held at both ends.

how: Sikhs who keep Nitnem say the Japji and Jaap with other banis in the morning, Rehras in the evening and Sohila before sleep; Sukhmani is read by many on its own, and Asa di Var is sung at dawn in gurdwaras.

o: the rules for how a gurdwara is run each day
a look back at the Guru's words that frame a Sikh day
the stories of the Gurus, told in the order they lived

games.q: a line from each — tap the pairs.
p: true in the beginning, through the ages
bliss has come, O my mother
the house where praise is sung

s: Sohila is the Sikh morning prayer
Sohila is said at night, before sleep. the Japji opens the morning.
the Jaap's opening says the One has no mark, color or caste
chakkar chihan ar baran jaat ar paat nahin jih.
the banis are one long prayer said all at once
they're separate hymns that frame the day: dawn, evening and the edge of sleep.

games.q: your cousin starts a night shift and gets home at dawn. she asks which bani goes at the end of her day. what fits?
o: Sohila, the bani for before sleep, whenever her sleep comes.
the Japji, since it's the first bani and the first is always best.
Asa di Var, since it's sung at dawn and she gets home at dawn.
games.why: the banis frame a day by what it's doing, not only the clock: Sohila is the prayer before sleep.

practice: Say a line from each out loud, slowly, the way Simran does between stops: aad sach; chakkar chihan; anand bhaiaa meri maae; so dar keha; jai ghar keerat aakheeai; sukhmani sukh amrit prabh naam; balihaari gur aapne.
Then go round once more, hearing which one stays.

wordCard.voice: Five years: the banis. The Guru's words that frame a Sikh day, from the Japji at dawn to Sohila at night.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the Guru's word; a hymn or prayer from the Gurus' writings.

carryVoice: For the road: the banis, seven lines on a school bus, a day held at both ends. That's the week, all six lines back in your pocket.
